title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
summary: The Great Wave off Kanagawa  is a woodblock print by the Japanese ukiyo-e artist Hokusai (1760–1849), created in late 1831 during the Edo period of Japanese history. The print depicts three boats moving through a storm-tossed sea, with a large, cresting wave forming a spiral in the centre over the boats and Mount Fuji in the background.

sections.name: the great wave's crest
sections.description: The massive, claw-like crest of the wave, frozen at its peak, symbolizes the overwhelming power of nature.

sections.name: Mount Fuji
sections.description: Mount Fuji, Japan's sacred mountain, appears small and calm, providing a focal point of stability amidst the storm.

sections.name: a cargo boat
sections.description: One of three cargo boats showing oarsmen huddled together as they navigate the dangerous swell.

museum_facts: Hokusai’s composition uses perspective to make Mount Fuji look like a small triangle nestled inside the hollow of the cresting wave.
The print is part of his *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji* series and dates to about 1830–32.
It is a Japanese woodblock print made with ink and color on paper, using a palette that includes indigo and imported Prussian blue.
The Met notes that the composition is said to have inspired Debussy’s *La Mer* and Rilke’s *Der Berg*.

guide_notes.the great wave's crest: Let your fingers climb the long raised arc that sweeps from the upper left and curls inward, the tallest thing in the whole relief. Along its outer lip the surface breaks into a row of small hooked ridges, each one lifted like a bent finger, and the space inside the curl is smoothed and hollowed, scooped lower than the paper around it. Feel how the little hooks repeat the shape of the big curve, again and again, until they thin out into scattered droplets. One thing the makers discovered only recently: when the Metropolitan Museum scanned the deep-blue hollow of this curl under a microscope, they found the blue was printed not once but twice, layer on layer, which is exactly why it sits lower than the untouched white paper around it.
guide_notes.Mount Fuji: Down near the centre of the relief, low and almost hidden beneath the great wave's arch, your fingertips will find a small, calm triangle with a gentle notched summit. Its flanks are smooth and low, and a band of raised white marks its snow-covered peak, set against a darker ground. Compare it with the wave you just touched: the mountain is barely the size of a thumbnail, and if you are not looking for it you might mistake it for one more crest. The surprise is that this tiny peak is the true subject of the whole series it belongs to, Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the dark tone around it is read by scholars as early-morning light just beginning to touch the snow.
guide_notes.a cargo boat: Run your fingers along the narrow hull low in the water, a thin curved ridge that rides in the trough between swells. Inside it you can feel a row of small rounded lumps packed tight, bent low over the sides, with thin straight lines running out from them that are the oars, and the whole boat feels small and pressed down beneath the towering water above. Everything about it is stretched and low, so that the sea seems to grow larger around it. Here is a detail most visitors never learn: these are oshiokuri-bune, fast barges built to rush fresh fish to market, and each one carried eight rowers plus two relief crew at the bow, so thirty men are meant to be in the scene but only twenty-two are actually drawn.
